utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. Can the interpreters hear me well?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you. Good afternoon to the Prosecution, counsel for the Defence, the court reporters. Good afternoon to Mr. Aleksovski as well. We are sitting today to resume our proceedings. Now that we have the decision of the Appeals Chamber, we are within the framework of Article 86 of our Rules, and I say that for the benefit of the public, to whom I also wish to say good afternoon. Rule 86 says that, after the presentation of all the evidence, the Prosecutor may present a rebuttal argument, to which the Defence may present a rejoinder. I think that we have to ask several questions before undertaking the closing arguments. During the Status Conference of the 20th of October, 1998, the Chamber asked the parties to submit their closing arguments in writing, in which they would specify the envisaged duration of their intervention for the closing arguments. The parties did not specify how long they intended to take. During the Status Conference of the 24th of August, 1998, the parties agreed to submit their final briefs on the same date, but they said nothing regarding the subject of a possible rebuttal and rejoinder after the closing arguments. The Chamber has reserved this afternoon and tomorrow morning for this sitting, in view of the fact that the parties have an extensive amount of work to cover in their written briefs, and so the Trial Chamber thought that this afternoon should be devoted to the Prosecution and tomorrow morning to the Defence. Nonetheless, we have two issues which I should like to address to the parties before they proceed with their closing arguments. The first question is, have the parties any idea regarding the envisaged time needed for the closing arguments? The second question is whether the parties intend to have a rebuttal or rejoinder or will they be content with the closing arguments? Those are the two preliminary questions that we should like to hear your responses to. Before answering this question, I should like the Prosecutor to speak first and then the Defence. Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. The way that we, the Prosecution, had intended to approach this matter was that I would address you on questions of law, and my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, would address you on questions of facts. It was my intention to speak for approximately an hour and three quarters, allowing then the time for the break, if there was to be a break. I understand that my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, will speak for approximately the same time. We will try and dispose of it in the course of this afternoon. I don't know whether Mr. Meddegoda will completely finish in that time, but if he does have to run over, he will, no doubt, at the time seek Your Honours' indulgence and take the matter up at that point. Your Honours, with respect to the question of the rebuttal case, it's hard for me at this stage to indicate whether or not we would be wanting to say anything to you in rebuttal, because, of course, as Your Honours appreciate, anything we say in rebuttal will arise out of matters which will be addressed by my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, in his address. I only envisage addressing Your Honours on matters which are new or haven't, in fact, been covered in any of the material that has been presented, either in our written address or in the addresses that we are about to deliver now. I would envisage, Your Honours, trying to traverse matters that have already been covered. We would leave it to Your Honours. If my colleague, Mr. Mikulicic, comes back with something contrary to what I've said -- I expect that to happen -- I would leave it to Your Honours then to determine which way to go on the matter. It's only if Mr. Mikulicic is to raise something which I haven't foreshadowed and it is of sufficient importance that I would seek to address you in rebuttal on those matters. Other than that, Your Honours, we would envisage taking up all of the time this afternoon at least for us to deliver our submissions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you also, at the same time, introduce the Prosecution team, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. I should have said that. Good afternoon, Your Honours. My name is Niemann. I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda, and Mr. Saxon is assisting us at the bar table today in place of Ms. Erasmus who is not available this afternoon, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, it is up to you to comment on the questions I have put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, my learned friends from the Prosecution. My name is Goran Mikulicic, and together with my friend, Mr. Joka, I am the Defence counsel for Mr. Aleksovski. In answer to your question, my reply would be as follows: The Defence plans, within a period of three hours, to complete its oral closing arguments. The Defence has not prepared in advance for any kind of rejoinder. However, should the need arise, and this would stem from any allegations or statements made on the Prosecution side, then naturally, the Defence will respond. Similarly, the Defence wishes to say that it will not go back to certain issues that have been covered in our written brief but that it will only focus on certain points which it considers to be of the greatest importance for judgement in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Marc Dubuisson, could you call the case, please, for the benefit of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Marc Dubuisson. I think that we can begin with our work, and we are going to organise ourselves as follows: We shall assume that we began at 2.00, because, from the standpoint of the interpreters, we did, indeed. We will work for one hour, ten minutes, after which we will have a 20-minute break, and then we will work again for another one-hour-and-ten-minute session, a 20-minute break, and then a period of work again, so that we know what the timetable is. Having stated that, I give the floor to Mr. Niemann to begin with his closing arguments. Mr. Niemann, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please. Your Honours, in this submission, I will try not to repeat matters which are dealt with in our written brief which we rely on fully as part of our closing address. I do want, Your Honours, to draw your attention to what I submit is a new and evolving legal issue relating to the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions and the questions of how we should deal with the issue of international armed conflict. Whereas in our closing brief, we have tended to take a traditional approach to this question, in this submission, I wish to examine what are perhaps more the frontiers of the law and try to enjoin Your Honours to participate in this important development. Before I do that, allow me to dwell upon some of the other significant issues concerning this case. Firstly, the question of what occurred in the Lasva Valley and what has often been referred to as ethnic cleansing: Your Honours, now that we have heard the evidence, it can be seen that the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, along with others, participated in a widespread scheme to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley of the Muslim population. The part of the operation that was occupied by Mr. Aleksovski was at the receiving end of the scheme, but this, in no way, detracts from the importance of his participation. It was his job to receive the Muslims in the Kaonik camp, to process them, and there, where they were subjected to such horrific conditions, that not only would they be desperate to get out of the Kaonik prison itself, but they would be so traumatised that they would want to leave the Lasva Valley altogether. Your Honours, it takes a determined effort to force human beings to give up their homes and lifelong possessions and go and live somewhere else, especially if your objective is to achieve this on a permanent basis. In some parts of the world, we see earthquakes, floods, fires, and other such natural disasters which strike with such ferocity and wreak so much damage that it's hard to imagine why people continue to live there afterwards. But such is the strength of their affiliation to their homelands that they persevere, notwithstanding these incredible events. Consider then for a moment just how much physical and psychological pain you would have to inflict to achieve this by ethnic cleansing. In 1993, this was the business of the accused and his associates. It's most unlikely that you will ever hear the Defence witnesses describe it as ethnic cleansing, especially if the witnesses were or are in positions of authority. This is something that, for the most part, we have to infer from the evidence. However, we do sometimes get glimpses of this plan, even when defence witnesses attempt to disguise and protect the interests of the authorities and governments, in this case, the government of the Republic of Croatia, and the government of the HVO. We do see from Defence witnesses this glimpse of what was occurring at that time. When we look at the evidence of the Defence witness Tomislav Rajic, page 3.187, line 23 of the transcript, he said: "However, in the spring of 1992, when the first but fairly numerous ... Muslims ... began to arrive, the refugees, there was a sort of demographic imbalance, the demographic balance was upset which had existed until that time ... This upset our cooperation and the events that followed took place." Later he was to describe the influx of Muslim refugees that had interrupted the ethnic balance as "drastic." That is at page 3.189 of the transcript. Although this was consistent with their somewhat bizarre and artificial theme to blame it all on the Serbs, it brazenly admits to their programme of ethnic readjustment based on discrimination. However, the facts put a lie to their claim that it was the ethnic imbalance which led to the events of 1993 because it wasn't the Muslim refugees from other areas of Bosnia, who were displaced by the Serbs, who were forced out of the Lasva Valley, it was the long-term Muslim residents of the area. Contrary to the Defence case which sought to impress upon us the racial tolerance allegedly possessed by the accused, we have the opposite version given in the evidence, for example, of the ECMM monitor, Mr. McLeod, where, in reference to the beating of Muslims by HVO soldiers, he quotes the accused Mr. Aleksovski as saying, "Would you shoot a man who has lost his brother to stop him from abusing Muslims?" See page 133 of the transcript. Large criminal enterprises such as that which occurred in the Lasva Valley in the first half of 1993 cannot be carried out by one person. It takes governments and large organisations to commit these crimes, governments whose acts are carried out by their willing servants. The acts of individual servants may only form a part of a much bigger and more sinister criminal act. Sometimes the dimensions of government crimes are so large-scale that the real content of the criminal behaviour becomes obscured by bureaucratic officialdom, but such officialdom should never be permitted to obscure the reality of the crime itself. The accused Aleksovski was one such willing servant. Of course, he didn't have all the power, he was not the most senior political or military figure in the region, but nonetheless his acts were an integral part of a larger crime. What then is the crime with which we are dealing? The Geneva Convention of 1949, picked up and applied by the Statute of this Tribunal, does not make the waging of a war a criminal offence. The concise position is this: War or armed conflict is not prohibited, but if engaged in, then it must be strictly according to the Geneva Conventions. Otherwise, the Conventions are breached and criminal liability will attach. In other words, it is not a defence to come before this Tribunal and say, "Well, we engaged in war or armed conflict, and we tried, where possible, to comply with the Geneva Conventions, but times were tough and so we could not do any better." This is not even a mitigating factor when it comes to sentencing. Under international law, if you must engage in war or if you must participate in armed conflict, then you must abide by the Geneva Conventions of 1949. When dealing with a similar argument by the Defence in the case of The Prosecutor v. Celebici in their judgement of the Trial Chamber, IT-96-21-T at paragraph 1.117, page 381, the Trial Chamber said as follows: "It is the position of the defence that, in light of the overall situation in the Konjic municipality at the time, no criminal liability can attach to the accused, as the conditions prevailing in the Celebici prison camp were the best that could be provided. The Trial Chamber must, as a matter of law, reject this view. As set out above, the legal standards here at issue are absolute, not relative. They delineate a minimum standard of treatment from which no derogation can be permitted. Accordingly, it is the Trial Chamber's view that a detaining power, or those acting on its behalf, cannot plead a lack of resources as a legal justification for exposing the individuals to conditions of detention that are inhumane." The contention that the conditions endured by the Kaonik detainees were no worse than those endured by the free Croatian community, Bosnian Croatian community, does not stand up to scrutiny in any event. The reality was that the free Bosnian Croatian community was not illegally arrested, they were not illegally detained, they were not sent to the front line to dig trenches when conditions were dangerous. The Bosnian Croatian volunteers and conscripts only worked at night when it was safer from the effects of snipers. They were not under armed guard, they were not forced to work hours on end without a break. For the most part, they were given the best protection that could be provided. For the Muslim Kaonik detainees, the evidence demonstrates that the conditions for them were quite the opposite. The term "ethnic cleansing" may not as such appear in the Geneva Conventions. It should not therefore be thought that this whole abhorrent business may somehow have slipped through the fingers of the parcel of prohibited conducts as prescribed by the Conventions. There is no question that the conduct necessary to achieve ethnic cleansing is well and truly prohibited by the Conventions. For instance, Article 49 of the Civilian Convention makes forcible transfer or deportations of civilians illegal. The grave breach provisions, Article 147, prohibits unlawful deportation, transfer, or confinement of protected persons. Common Article 3 prohibits adverse distinction of persons based on race, colour, religion, or other similar criteria. Therefore, there is no question that the acts necessary to effect ethnic cleansing are themselves prohibited, and this, in turn, is properly reflected in the various charges in the indictment. Accordingly, if, in the course of ethnic cleansing or in order to achieve ethnic cleansing, you subject people to inhumane treatment, if you wilfully cause great suffering or serious injury to body or health, or if you inflict outrages upon the personal dignity, then this conduct is directly prohibited by the Conventions. Accordingly, it was, in our submission, manifestly illegal to round up the civilian Muslim population of the Busovaca and Vitez municipalities and then illegally intern them in the Kaonik prison solely on the basis of their ethnicity. When these people were illegally interned in the Kaonik prison, it was manifestly illegal to beat them; to deprive them of proper food, hygiene, and medical treatment; to overcrowd them under inhumane conditions; to deprive them of proper bedding and warmth. It was manifestly illegal to send them to the front in dangerous conditions, and there to force them to dig trenches for the HVO. When at the front, it was manifestly illegal to rob them and abuse them. It was manifestly illegal to force them to work for hours on end without adequate rest or nutrition. Dealing now with the question of the illegal confinement of civilians. The question of the illegality of the confinement of civilians can be a difficult matter if the State can justify that they represented a serious threat to the State, but the threat has to be real. As noted again in the Celebici judgement, paragraph 1.134, page 387, Their Honours said: "... the Trial Chamber is convinced that a significant number of the civilians were detained in the Celebici camp although there existed no serious and legitimate reason to conclude that they seriously prejudiced the security of the detaining power. To the contrary, it appears that the confinement of the civilians in the Celebici camp was a collective measure aimed at a specific group of persons based mainly on their ethnic background and not as a legitimate security measure." As Your Honours remember, in that case, they were Serb detainees. "As stated above --" I'm quoting on from the Trial Chamber's decision. " -- the mere fact that a person is a national of or aligned with an enemy party cannot be considered as threatening the security of the opposing party where he is living and therefore be a valid reason for interning him." Your Honours, the evidence in this case bears this out even more than what was the case in Celebici because the fact is that in this case some people were sent home from time to time. "Well, they're allowed to go home with one of the guards," which all suggests that they could not have in any way been a serious threat to the HVO. Turning now to the issue of human shields. With respect to the use of detainees as human shields, Article 28 of the Civilian Geneva Convention 4 of 1949 provides that the presence of protected persons may not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations. Similarly, Article 23 of the Prisoners of War Third Geneva Convention provides that the presence of prisoners of war shall not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations. Both of these provisions need to be read in conjunction with Article 50, paragraph 7, of the 1977 Additional Protocol 1, which provides that the presence or movements of the civilian population or individuals shall not be used to render certain points or areas immune from military operations, in particular in attempts to shield military objectives from attacks or to shield, favour, or impede military operations. The parties to the conflict shall not direct the movement of civilian populations or individual civilians in order to attempt to shield military objectives from attacks or to shield military operations. The net effect of these provisions is that using people as human shields is illegal and contrary to the Geneva Conventions and the Additional Protocols of 1977. Therefore, the use of the Muslim prisoners at the Kaonik prison camp as human shields in 1993 was manifestly illegal. Turning now to the question of international armed conflict. In the judgement of the Trial Chamber in The Prosecution v. Zejnil Delalic, the Celebici case, of the 16th of November, 1998, the Trial Chamber said, paragraph 202, page 76: "While Trial Chamber II in the Tadic case did not initially consider the nature of the armed conflict to be a relevant consideration in applying Article 2 of the Statute, the majority of the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdictional decision did find that the grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions could be only committed in international armed conflicts and this requirement was thus an integral part of Article 2 of the Statute." In his separate opinion, however, Judge Abi-Saad opined that "a strong case can be made for the application of Article 2 of the Statute even when the incriminated acts take place in an internal conflict. The Appeals Chamber did indeed recognise that a change in the customary law scope of the 'grave breach regimes' in this direction may be occurring. This Trial Chamber is also of the view that the possibility that customary law has developed the provisions of the Geneva Conventions since 1949 to constitute an extension of the system of 'grave breaches' to internal armed conflicts should be recognised." Your Honours, this advance in the law was picked up and advanced even a little further very recently in the jurisdictional decision of Trial Chamber III in The Prosecutor v. Dario Kordic and another, IT-95-14/2-PT of the 2nd of March, 1999, when the Trial Chamber, paragraph 15, acknowledged with approval the step taken in Celebici. Perhaps more interestingly, at paragraph 31, when considering the Additional Protocols of the Geneva Conventions of 1977, including Protocol 1 which, as Your Honours know, is the protocol dealing with international armed conflicts, Trial Chamber III says this: "There is no possible doubt as to the customary status of these specific provisions as they reflect core principles of humanitarian law that can be considered as applying to all armed conflicts whether intended to apply to international or non-international conflicts." Thus, in my respectful submission, Trial Chamber III has taken the advance of unhesitatingly expressing the customary status of the Additional Protocols, including Protocol 1, with respect to their application to conflicts irrespective of whether the conflict is internal or international. Accordingly, in my submission, it is only logical that the grave breach provisions of the Conventions in themselves, which are, in fact, older in time, should also, without doubt, enjoy such customary status. All it takes is for Your Honours to say so. I will now endeavour to assist Your Honours in giving you at least one path for you to consider in reaching what I submit is the sensible and inevitable result. At the outset, let me say that on the evidence, the existence of an international armed conflict at the relevant times and place has, we say, been unquestionably proved beyond a reasonable doubt, so that any advance that Your Honours might make in the law can in no way affect the position of the accused. When considering the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions, it is interesting to compare these Conventions with the Convention on genocide. Article 6 of the Genocide Convention of 1948 provides that: "... persons charged with genocide ... shall be tried ... by a ... State or international penal tribunal ... which States have accepted its jurisdiction." Article 8 allows States to call upon the United Nations to take appropriate action. Clearly, the drafters of the Genocide Convention contemplated that it would have a truly international enforcement mechanism. International in the sense that international bodies would play a direct part in the Convention's enforcement. Thus, international tribunals would play a part in the prevention and suppression of acts of genocide. This Genocide Convention stands in stark contrast to the four Geneva Conventions of 1949 which makes no reference to "International Tribunals." The four Geneva Conventions contemplated international enforcement, but enforcement would be undertaken by States on behalf of the International Community. There is no suggestion of this being done by international tribunals, as is the case with the Genocide Conventions. Accordingly, if the Statute of this Tribunal did not expressly refer to the Geneva Conventions of 1949 in Article 2, then the Tribunal would only have jurisdiction with respect to the Conventions if the Conventions, and more particularly the "grave breach" provision, had become part of international customary law. This being so, the Geneva Conventions as drafted were expressly intended to be enforced by States. As the Appeals Chamber noted in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal, page 46, paragraph 80: "The international armed conflict element generally attributed to the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions is merely a function of the system of universal mandatory jurisdiction that those provisions create. The international armed conflict requirement was a necessary limitation on the grave breaches system in light of the intrusion on State sovereignty that such mandatory universal jurisdiction represents. State parties to the 1949 Geneva Conventions did not want to give other States jurisdiction over serious violations of international law committed in their internal conflicts, at least not the mandatory universal jurisdiction involved in the grave breach system." However, this Tribunal is not concerned with the issue of State sovereignty. Under Article 2, paragraph 7 of the United Nations Charter, "the United Nations shall not interfere with matters which are essentially within the domestic jurisdiction of any State." But measures under Chapter 7 are expressly excluded from this general restriction. This Tribunal was created by the Security Council as a Chapter 7 measure. Furthermore, the Statute of the Tribunal expressly gives it jurisdiction by virtue of Article 8 of our Statute. Article 8, "Territorial Jurisdiction," is as broad as could be enjoyed by any State court in the exercise of domestic jurisdiction. The Statute goes even further and gives the Tribunal jurisdiction much wider than that even enjoyed by most State courts because Article 9, paragraph 2, provides that the Tribunal, in the exercise of its jurisdiction, shall have primacy over State courts, and Article 10, paragraph 1, limits the jurisdiction of State courts. In light of these Articles, it is hard to imagine a more intrusive jurisdictional limitation on the sovereignty of a State. Indeed, it becomes absurd, in my submission, to speak of the need to respect State sovereignty by not applying the grave breach provisions until and unless an international armed conflict is established because of a concern not to intrude into the sovereignty of another State, yet at the same time expressly asserting primacy over the courts of that very same State. It's interesting that even States themselves are not quite so concerned about sovereignty when the fate of innocent human beings is at stake. Even the Geneva Conventions themselves relegates State sovereignty to second place in cases of doubt. For example, Article 5 of the Geneva Convention 3 contemplates that a State court will exercise jurisdiction and assume, in cases of doubt, that the Conventions apply unless the contrary is established. This is consistent with how most domestic courts operate on jurisdictional matters. The Prosecution rarely has to prove jurisdiction beyond a reasonable doubt as an element of the offence. The Prosecution brings the case, and the Defence can challenge jurisdiction and endeavour to prove, on the balance of probabilities, that the courts do not have jurisdiction. This approach was clearly contemplated by Rule 72(A)(i) of the Tribunal's own Rules which contemplates challenges to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal as being a preliminary issue.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Further, when dealing with the whole question of the decline of State sovereignty, I could find no more eloquent expression than that contained in the Tadic Jurisdictional Appeal Judgement itself when the majority held, at page 54, paragraph 97, where Their Honours said: "... A State-sovereignty approach has been gradually supplanted by a human-being-oriented approach ... It follows that in the area of armed conflict, the distinction between interstate and civil wars is losing value as far as human beings are concerned." The Appeals Chamber then goes on to pose the rhetorical question: "Why protect civilians from belligerent violence or ban rape, et cetera ... when two sovereign States are engaged in war, and yet refrain from enacting the same bans ... when armed violence has erupted only within the territory of the sovereign State?" The Appeals Chamber then answers: "If international law, while of course duly safeguarding the legitimate interests of States, must gradually turn to the protection of human beings, it is only natural that the aforementioned dichotomy should gradually lose its weight." At page 64, paragraph 119, the Appeals Chamber declares as preposterous the notion that weapons prohibited in international armed conflict may not be prohibited in internal armed conflict. The grave breach provisions are at the very heart of the Geneva Conventions. Their application is essential to the continued operations of these most important Conventions. When considering this matter, we should ask ourselves the following questions: Is it appropriate that everything should hang on the classification of the conflict as being international? Should otherwise clearly guilty war criminals escape conviction and punishment because there exists politically motivated arguments, often promulgated by the guilty warring States themselves who are anxious to avoid the imposition of war reparations or other consequences by having the conflict internal rather than international in character? The issue of the classification of the conflict has, in my submission, nothing to do with the individual participants. It is a matter of concern only to the State involved. Do you think that the classification of the conflict was a factor which weighed heavily on the mind of an accused person when he or she was about to commit a crime contrary to the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions? More importantly, do you think that the victims of those crimes would feel that an acquittal, based on the fact that the conflict was arguably internal, would, in their mind, constitute justice? Would such a technical, artificial, irrelevant, and unsatisfactory conclusion generally contribute to reconciliation and restoration of peace in the former Yugoslavia? In the Celebici decision again, the Trial Chamber, in my submission, very correctly interpreted the Geneva Conventions when it cited with approval the commentary on the 4th Geneva Convention, paragraph 263: "The Commentary to the Fourth Geneva Convention charges us not to forget that 'The Conventions have been drawn up first and foremost to protect individuals and not to serve State interests,' and thus it is the view of the Trial Chamber that their protection should be applied to as broad a category of persons as possible." If the classification of the conflict as an international conflict had to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt as an element of the offence and that this was the unequivocal state of the law, then I guess the answer to all these questions might have to be "Yes," irrespective of the fact that they may be artificial or irrespective of the fact that they may be irrelevant. However, in my respectful submission, this is not the case. It has not been expressly stated anywhere that the classification of the conflict is an element of the offence which has to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. Why do I say this? As I've stated above, the 1949 Geneva Conventions had not envisaged that the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions would be enforced by an International Tribunal, such as this Tribunal. Accordingly, the whole focus of their attention was on the Conventions being enforced by State courts. State courts are justifiably concerned with exercising jurisdiction over events that occurred in the territory of another State. An instance, for example, is the caution taken by the High Court in Britain recently over the arrest of General Pinochet. One of the primary issues at the heart of the matter was should a British court try a person in Britain for crimes committed in Chile. This reluctance is not limited to British courts but operates throughout the world. When the drafters of the Geneva Conventions introduced the idea that State courts would enforce the grave breach provisions, they had to address the issue of enforcement by State courts, other than the State where the crimes were committed because they were acutely aware of the reluctance of State courts to interfere with another State court's jurisdiction. In an effort to assuage this concern by State courts, they introduced a number of measures to encourage State courts to accept jurisdiction. The primary issue was whether or not the conflict was international or internal. If it was international, the drafters figured that the problem would be solved because the objection to State courts intruding on the exclusive jurisdiction of another State court disappeared, that is, if it is international, it is not the exclusive jurisdiction of one State, so that another State could exercise jurisdiction. What then has this got to do with the Tribunal? In my submission, absolutely nothing. The very important question we should ask ourselves is this: Is it appropriate for reasons of comity for this Tribunal to be hesitant about exercising jurisdiction over persons responsible for serious violations of international humanitarian law, which include grave breaches committed in the territory of the former Yugoslavia since 1991? I sincerely hope not. It is the whole purpose of our being. It is the mandate laid down for us by the Security Council. Indeed, it's the very thing that is expected of us. As observed by the Trial Chamber in the Celebici judgement, paragraph 263, Their Honours said: "It would be contrary to the intention of the Security Council, which was concerned with effectively addressing the situation that it had determined to be a threat to international peace and security, and with ending the suffering of all those caught up in the conflict, for the International Tribunal to deny the application of the Fourth Geneva Convention to any particular group of persons solely on the basis of their citizenship status under domestic law." The fact that the drafters of the Tribunal Statute gave the Tribunal territorial and temporal jurisdiction under Article 8 and primacy over State courts in Article 9(2) leads, in my submission, to the inescapable conclusion that the Security Council intended the Tribunal to get on with its mandate and not concern itself with the kind of sovereignty issues that inhibit State courts from exercising jurisdiction under similar circumstances. Clearly, in my submission, that is why Article 2 of the Tribunal Statute, which incorporates the grave breach provisions as part of the offence provisions of the Statute, makes no mention of international armed conflict. Thus to maintain the view that an international armed conflict must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt as an element of the offence before the Tribunal can exercise jurisdiction is, in my submission, wrong at law. In our submission, it is also quite erroneous, as a matter of law, for the Defence to assert that the international armed conflict has to reach down to the very place where the crime was committed. In our submission, the Prosecution has no legal obligation to prove that the Republic of Croatia or the HV were, in any way, directly involved in the running of the Kaonik prison facility, or that the prisoners were gathered up by the HV, or that somehow Mr. Aleksovski was employed by the HV, or even that the HVO ran the Kaonik facility as agents for the Republic of Croatia or the HV. When dealing with the parameters of the conflict, again the Celebici Trial Chamber expressed the following opinion, page 79, paragraph 209; they said: "Before proceeding any further, the Trial Chamber deems it necessary to address the possibility that there may be some confusion as to the parameters of this concept of an international armed conflict. We are not here examining the Konjic municipality and the particular forces involved in the conflict in that area to determine whether it was international or internal. Rather, should the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina be international, the relevant norms of international humanitarian law apply throughout its territory until the general cessation of hostilities, unless it can be shown that the conflict in some areas were separate internal conflicts unrelated to the larger international armed conflict."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, excuse me for interrupting you, but I see on the English transcript, there is a reference to "Kaonik municipality," and I heard "Konjic municipality."

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: It should be "Konjic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I don't know if that's a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I'm quoting from Their Honours' decision, and it's "Konjic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well. You may continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. The Trial Chamber in Celebici continue, at page 80, paragraph 212, to say: "The JNA had been providing arms and equipment to the Serb population in Bosnia-Herzegovina since 1991, who had in turn been organising themselves into various units and militia in preparation for combat. Similarly, the Bosnian Croats had been receiving such support from the Government of Croatia and its armed forces." Again, in paragraph 213, they say: "The United Nations Security Council and the European Community recognised this involvement of these and other outside forces in the conflict by calling for the Governments of Croatia and Serbs to exert 'their undoubted influence' in demanding the cessation of all forms of outside interference." In paragraph 214 and 215, they conclude: "On the basis of this evidence alone, the Trial Chamber can conclude that an international armed conflict existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the date of its recognition as an independent State on 6 April, 1992. There is no evidence to indicate the hostilities which occurred in the Konjic municipality at that time were part of a separate armed conflict, and indeed there is some evidence of the involvement of the JNA in the fighting there. It is evident that there was no general cessation of hostilities in Bosnia-Herzegovina until the signing of the Dayton Peace Agreement in November 1995." Likewise, in my submission, there is no evidence to indicate that the hostilities which occurred in the Busovaca and Vitez municipalities were part of a separate armed conflict, and, indeed, there is some evidence of the involvement of the HV in the fighting there. We have evidence of the rounding up of the Muslim civilians by members of the HV, and we certainly have evidence of a connection between the two armies of the HVO and the HV. Professor Bianchini expressed the opinion that, for all intents and purposes, they were the same army. Again, in the Celebici judgement, the Trial Chamber made a number of interesting findings about the nature of the participants to the conflict. In paragraph 187, page 72, they refer to the JNA which became the VJ and the VRS which was controlled by the Bosnian Serb administration in Pale. They then go on to say: "The HVO was in a similar position to the VRS, in that it was established by the self-proclaimed para-state of the Bosnian Croats as its army and operated from territory under its control." Moreover, the Trial Chamber, in reaching its conclusion that an international armed conflict did exist on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time in the Celebici judgement, declined to follow the decision of the majority in the Tadic case, considered that the Nicaragua case was not appropriate as a source of authority, having regard to the nature of the proceedings, and fully accepted the dissenting judgement of Judge McDonald, as she then was, on this issue of the involvement of the JNA in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is not the first time that such a decision has been made. In the Rajic Rule 61 hearing, IT-95-12-R61, at page 9, paragraph 13, the Trial Chamber said: "The Chamber finds that for the purposes of the application of the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Convention 4, the significant and continuous military action by the armed forces of Croatia in support of the Bosnian Croats against the forces of the Bosnian government on the territory of the latter was sufficient to convert the domestic conflict between the Bosnian Croats and the Bosnian Government into an international one." Nor is there any basis to the suggestion by the Defence, through the evidence of Admiral Domazet and others, that the presence of the forces of the Republic of Croatia were merely there because it had to protect border regions of Croatia on the Dalmacija coast and the Krajina. Again in the Rajic Rule 61 hearing, this ruse mounted by the Republic of Croatia did not fool the Trial Chamber because, at page 12, paragraph 19, it held: "The material before the Trial Chamber also suggests that, contrary to Croatia's claims, Croatian troops were not just stationed in border areas and that they were involved in hostilities against the Bosnian --" I'm sorry "and that they were involved in hostilities against the Bosnian Government forces in central and southern Bosnia." Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal does, however, make reference to the protected person provisions of the Geneva Conventions. In an examination of these provisions, it does not show international armed conflict as part of the definition of protected persons and property. Further, no analysis of the meaning of "protected persons" would be complete without looking at the definition of "protected persons and property" as contained in the Protocol Additional to the Geneva Convention of 1949. Paragraph 4 of Article 1 of Protocol 1 extends the ambit of conflict to persons involved in struggles for self-determination against colonial domination, alien occupation, or racist regimes. All or any of these could be in the context of an internal armed conflict, thus supporting the argument that the definition of "protected persons" is not entirely limited to persons involved in international armed conflict. Interestingly enough, Additional Protocol 1, Paragraph 3 of Article 1, expressly provides that the Protocol supplement the Geneva Conventions of 1949. Clearly, Article 1(4) of Protocol 1 severs the 1949 Article 2 definition from what was then strictly "international armed conflicts." Likewise, the definition of "Prisoner of War" has been expanded by Protocol 1. Article 43 of the Additional Protocol expands the party to the conflict to the armed forces of a party which may not be recognised by the other party to the conflict. Article 44 of the 1977 Protocols provides that any combatant covered by the expanded definition in Article 43 who falls into the hands of an adverse party shall be a prisoner of war. If there was ever any doubt that the prisoners of war interned at the Kaonik prison came within the definition of prisoner of war by virtue of the 1949 Geneva Conventions, then that doubt has been completely resolved by the prisoner of war definitions as contained in the 1977 Additional Protocols. Similarly, what is meant by the term "protected persons" in Article 4 of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 dealing with civilians would not be complete without looking to Article 50 and 51 of Additional Protocol 1 of 1977. Article 50 provides that a civilian is any person who is not defined as a prisoner of war by either the Third Geneva Conventions of 1949 or by the Additional Protocol. Article 50 makes no distinction whatsoever based on nationality or otherwise. Accordingly, in my submission, there is no basis for defining nationality as it appears in Article 4 of the Fourth Convention as something intrinsically linked to only a conflict of an international character. Clearly it must mean something more than that. In my submission, the only logical conclusion is that it means "civilian" as defined in Article 50 of Additional Protocol 1. Accordingly, there is no question that the Muslims of Busovaca and Vitez, who were non-combatants, a sizeable proportion of whom found themselves imprisoned in Kaonik, were civilians within the meaning of Article 50 of Protocol 1 and were thus protected persons under the Fourth Geneva Conventions. Is that a convenient time, Your Honour? Does Your Honour want me to continue on? I'm mindful of the time. I think you said one hour and ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I was dealing with the definition of "civilians" under Geneva Conventions, if Your Honours please. In dealing with this question of what constitutes a civilian under the Fourth Geneva Conventions, in the Celebici judgement, paragraph 245, page 92, the Trial Chamber begin with an examination of the reasoning of the Tadic judgement which, as I stated above, they declined to follow. They interpreted the Tadic judgement in the following way: They say that the connection between the individuals being in the hands of a party of a foreign nationality and the classification of the conflict is a key factor in the reasoning in Tadic because if the individuals were in the hands of captors of the same nationality, the conflict could not be international. They observed, however, at paragraph 251, that an analysis of the nationality laws of Bosnia-Herzegovina does not reveal a clear picture. At the time, the State was struggling to achieve its independence. In addition, an "international armed conflict was tearing Bosnia-Herzegovina apart, and the very issue which was being fought over concerned the desire of certain ethnic groups within its population to separate themselves from that State and join with another State." After concluding that the Bosnian Serbs in the hands of Bosnia-Herzegovina were protected persons for the purposes of the Fourth Geneva Convention, the Trial Chamber said at paragraph 265: " ... it is clear that the victims of the acts alleged in the indictment were arrested and detained mainly on the basis of their Serb identity. As such and insofar as they were not protected by any of the Geneva Conventions, they must be considered to have been 'protected persons' within the meaning of the Fourth Geneva Convention as they were regarded by the Bosnian authorities as belonging to the opposing party in an armed conflict and as posing a threat to the Bosnian State." This interpretation of the Convention is fully in accordance with the development of the human rights doctrine which has been increasing in force since the middle of this century. It would be incongruous that the whole concept of human rights, which protects individuals from the excesses of their own governments, to rigidly apply the nationality requirement of Article 4 that was apparently inserted to prevent interference in a State's relations with its own nationals. They then quote with approval from Professor Meron when they say". " ... in interpreting international law, our goal should be to avoid paralysing the legal process as much as possible and, in the case of humanitarian conventions, to enable them to serve their protective goals." After finding that the Bosnian Serb detainees at the Celebici camp were protected persons, at paragraph 275 the Trial Chamber then goes on: "This finding is strengthened by the Trial Chamber's fundamental conviction that the Security Council, in persistently condemning the widespread violations of international humanitarian law committed throughout the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina and indeed in establishing this International Tribunal to prosecute and punish such violations, did not consider that the protection of the whole corpus of international humanitarian law could be denied to particular groups of individuals on the basis of the provisions of domestic citizenship legislation. The International Tribunal must therefore take a broad and principled approach to the application of the basic norms of international humanitarian law, norms which are enunciated in the four Geneva Conventions. In particular, all those individuals who took no active part in hostilities and yet found themselves engulfed in the horror and violence of war should not be denied the protection of the Fourth Geneva Convention which constitutes the very basis of the law concerned with such persons." How then do we interpret what the Appeals Chamber meant when it said in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal at page 46, paragraph 81, that the reference to "protected persons and property," as set out in the various "protected persons and property" Articles of the Conventions, determines that these persons are only protected if they are perforce of those provisions caught in an international armed conflict," and that "... Article 2 of the (Tribunal) Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of an international armed conflict"? Not everything that occurs in the course of a criminal trial has to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. The only matters that do have to be proved by the Prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt are those matters which constitute the elements of the offence. Accordingly, if the Prosecution fails to satisfy the Tribunal of a fact beyond a reasonable doubt as to an essential element of the offence, then the accused is entitled to an acquittal. At no stage did the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal say that the finding of an international armed conflict was an essential element of the offence that must be proved beyond a reasonable doubt by the Prosecution. In the course of almost all criminal trials there arises issues of law which have to be decided upon as questions of fact. One example is an objection raised by the Defence to the admission of a piece of evidence on the grounds of its relevance. The decision of whether or not the evidence is relevant is a legal question. The basis of that legal question is grounded in fact. Accordingly, the Court hears argument and looks to other evidence and to the details of the particular piece of disputed evidence itself, and upon looking at all these bits and pieces of evidence, a legal determination is made as to whether the evidence is relevant or not. The facts adduced in support of the argument that a particular piece of evidence is relevant do not have to go so far as to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt. In the Celebici judgement, paragraph 602, page 214, referred in passing to this issue of the burden and standard of proof in certain circumstances. Their Honours say: "The burden is different when the accused makes the allegation ..." And then the important part which I wish to emphasise: " ... or when the allegation made by the Prosecutor is not an essential element of the charges in the indictment." Their Honours say: "In such a situation, the legal burden in a civil case will satisfy the standard required ..." This standard is, of course, the balance of probabilities or the preponderance of the evidence. Other examples of this would include various of the allegations as contained in the indictment. With respect to some of these particular allegations, the Prosecution would seek to prove them on a balance of probabilities but would not have to satisfy you beyond a reasonable doubt. By way of illustration, paragraph 7 of the indictment sets out particulars of the accused. It says that his parents are Tale and Eva. For identification purposes of the accused, it may very well be useful for the Prosecution to prove that his parents were, in fact, Tale and Eva. But if this was not proved beyond a reasonable doubt, the accused would not, on this basis, be entitled to an acquittal. There is no question that the way the Geneva Conventions were drafted it was intended that the grave breach provisions would operate in the context of an international armed conflict, and I explain that the reason for this was so that State courts could exercise universal jurisdiction. Further, the "protected persons" would be persons who found themselves caught up in an international armed conflict. I do not dispute this and I could not dispute it having regard to the wording and construction of the Conventions. However, in this case, the Prosecution asserts that the existence of an international armed conflict in Bosnia in 1993 is more in the nature of a background jurisdictional component of the charge which is a legal question and does not have to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt in order for the accused to be convicted. Having regard to the fact that the international armed conflict requirement is only an issue for States exercising extra-territorial jurisdiction and in no way impedes the jurisdiction of an international tribunal and having regard to the fact that Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal makes no reference to "international armed conflict," then it is my submission that proving the existence of an international armed conflict cannot be an essential ingredient of the charge. Whether or not it becomes an essential prerequisite for a State court exercising jurisdiction is fortunately not a matter that we have to be concerned with in this jurisdiction. Accordingly, because proof of the existence of an international armed conflict is not, in our submission, an essential element of the offence that has to be proved by the Prosecution beyond a reasonable doubt, a failure to so prove would not entitle the accused to an acquittal. The existence of an international armed conflict goes to the background legal question of jurisdiction. The facts that the Tribunal must consider in order to reach this determination do not have to reach the level where the matter is decided according to the criminal standard. The Tribunal can take into account a number of facts, not necessarily only those introduced by the Prosecution. It is permissible for the Judges of the Trial Chamber to draw upon their general knowledge and general life experiences. This is why, in my submission, the Appeals Chamber in Tadic is very careful in its selection of words on this point. The Appeals Chamber does not say "elements of the offence" when they are speaking of international armed conflict, they say, at paragraph 84, page 48: " ... Article 2 of the Statute only applies to offences committed within the context of an international armed conflict." And the emphasis, if Your Honours please, that I place is on the word "context." Thus, when looking at this particular conflict, what evidence is sufficient for you to resolve whether or not the conflict was international as a background jurisdictional question? The answer to the question is straightforward. The conflict becomes international in character if any difference arising between two States and leading to the intervention of members of the armed forces of that State is an international armed conflict, and it makes no difference how long the conflict lasts or how much slaughter takes place. They do not have to have a controlling influence or that they were present right across the territory of the particular State. Once this is established, in my submission, on the balance of probabilities, Article 2 of the Statute applies. You can then turn to the elements of the offence in order for you to determine whether it has been established beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused intended to subject the Bosnian Muslim detainees to inhumane treatment or to wilfully cause great suffering or serious injury to body or health under either Article 7(1) or 7(3). Your Honours, in this case, there is an abundance of evidence showing that the Republic of Croatia had military forces in Bosnia. They came in 1992 and they stayed on beyond 1993. There is no question that the military forces of Croatia were linked to the HVO which was the organisation of the Bosnian Croats. There is no question that the HVO was in conflict with the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1993. This is as far as you need to go in order to decide the background jurisdictional fact with respect to the grave breach provisions. Of course, you have before you a great deal more evidence than that, but this is all you need. Certainly you have a vastly greater amount of evidence before you than did the Appeals Chamber in the Tadic jurisdictional appeal when they, in fact, decided that the conflict in the former Yugoslavia had been rendered international by the involvement of the Croatian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina. This is at page 39, paragraph 72. Likewise, you have considerably more evidence before you than did the Trial Chamber in the Rajic Rule 61 hearing when the Trial Chamber said that the evidence was sufficient to convert a domestic conflict into an international one (paragraph 13, page 9). The same question was decided by the Celebici Trial Chamber when it said that there was an international armed conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the date of its recognition of independence on the 6th of April, 1992, until the signing of the Dayton peace agreement in November of 1994 (sic). Accordingly, when Your Honours come to consider this question, it will have been considered and decided at least four times. Of course, there is nothing different this time, and in view of the fact that on the previous four occasions it was decided that there did exist an international armed conflict, there is no reason why Your Honours need depart from this consistently held view. If Your Honours follow the line of reasoning in the other cases and having regard to what I have said above, I do not think that you will have much difficulty in concluding that an international armed conflict did exist in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time. Your Honours could, however, go further by applying the same reasoning that I have advanced above, about this being an issue for State courts and it not being expressly mentioned in Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal, and decide that Article 2 of the Statute of the Tribunal applies equally to internal and international armed conflicts. In the Celebici judgement, the Trial Chamber considered the possibility of expressing themselves on this issue but ultimately declined to do so at page 88, paragraph 235, of their judgement, when they say: "Having reached this conclusion, the Trial Chamber makes no finding on the question of whether Article 2 of the Statute can only be applied in a situation of an international armed conflict or whether this provision is also applicable to internal armed conflicts." I think, Your Honours -- I've been corrected. The Dayton Accords were signed in 1995. If I said 1994, I was wrong in that. Turning, Your Honours, to the issue of command responsibility. Again, in the Celebici judgement, the Trial Chamber stated, paragraph 346, page 128, that the elements that have to be satisfied in order to establish Article 7(3) responsibility were: (i) The existence of a superior-subordinate relationship; (ii) that the superior knew or had reason to know that the criminal act was about to be or had been committed; and (iii) the superior failed to take the necessary and reasonable measures to prevent the criminal act or to punish the perpetrators thereof. In Celebici, they went on to observe the situation in the former Yugoslavia, where formal structures had broken down, improvised control and command structures took their place. These improvised structures were often ambiguous and ill-defined, but this factor alone did not preclude the application of the doctrine of superior responsibility under Article 7(3). Provided it could be established that persons were effectively in control of these improvised structures with the power to prevent and punish the crimes of persons who are, in fact, under their control, may be held responsible for their failure to do so. Accordingly, individuals, whether in civilian or military structures, can incur criminal liability under the doctrine of superior responsibility on the basis of their de facto as well as their de jure positions as superiors. The mere absence of formal legal authority to control the actions of subordinates will not preclude criminal responsibility. Thus, it is apparent that there is no express limitation restricting the scope of superior responsibility to military commanders or situations arising under military command. In contrast, the use of the term "superior" in Article 7(3), juxtaposition to the affirmation of individual criminal responsibility of "Heads of State" or responsible government in Article 7(2), clearly indicates that this applicability extends beyond the responsibility of military commanders to also encompass political leaders and other civilian superiors in positions of authority. In the case of the United States versus Oswald Pohl, reported at Volume V, T.W.C. 958, the finding of guilt against the accused, who was an officer of the Waffen SS and a business manager of a large establishment of industries employing concentration camp labour, is best read as predicated upon his possession of de facto powers of control. Charged with his responsibility for the conditions to which labourers were exposed, he based his defence in part on the contention that any mistreatment of prisoners was caused by the concentration camp guards over whom he had no control. This was rejected by the Nuremberg Tribunal when it found that he was an integral part of the whole concentration camp process. If excesses occurred in industries under his control, he not only knew about it but he could do something. Accordingly, powers of influence, not amounting to formal powers of command, is sufficient basis for the imposition of command responsibility. Cases imposing criminal responsibility for failure to act on civilian positions of authority also indicate that such persons may be liable for crimes committed by persons over whom their formal authority under national law is limited or nonexistent. Whatever the Defence might say about the de jure authority of Mr. Aleksovski, we have evidence that "shift commanders could not make instructions on their own. They had to receive instructions from the warden"; transcript page 3.034. We also have an abundance of Mr. Aleksovski giving orders to guards. He even gave orders to the guards to beat prisoners; transcript page 1.389. It is nonsense, in my submission, to suggest that he did not have control over the guards of the camp. He was the warden, he had the responsibility to run the place, and the only way that he could have done this was by his control over the camp personnel, including the guards. If a person is a superior and has authority to influence an event, he cannot plead lack of formal or de jure authority as a defence when he failed to take this action. Thus, if the superior is superior in his position to those who perpetrate the acts, if he has the requisite knowledge of the occurrence of those events and fails to do what was within his powers to either prevent further crimes or punish the perpetrators thereof, then in those circumstances he is guilty under the principle of command responsibility. It is of no avail for him to say, "Well, I was the warden of the prison --"
