utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, it is of no avail for the accused to say, "Well, I was the warden of the prison. I knew that the detainees were being mistreated contrary to the provisions of the Geneva Conventions, but those guards were not under my command because I was attached to the Justice Department and the guards were attached to the Defence Department." The fact is that he could act if he wanted to. For example, when the two Muslim detainees Ermin Elezovic and Jasmin Sehovic were taken out for trench-digging, mistreated and ultimately murdered, he did not claim lack of authority; he took appropriate action by initiating a formal investigation, demonstrating that he was far from powerless. The Defence would have you believe that unless you had complete de jure authority over the destiny of his subordinates, then Article 7(3) of the Statute has no application. This is simply not true. Nor is it true to say that Article 7(3) only applies to situations where he can take direct punitive action. There are a great many things he could have done. He could have gave the guards an order not to beat the detainees rather than doing the opposite and ordering them to beat the prisoners. He could have avoided giving the guards a bad example when he himself joined in when prisoners were beaten. He could have reported the guards for beating the prisoners. He could have told the ECMM Monitors what was happening. He could have told the International Committee of the Red Cross about the plight of the Muslim detainees instead of lying to them, when they asked who was in the locked cell, and he covered up by saying that the cell contained stored food when, in fact, it contained a prisoner who had been badly beaten; transcript page 1.472. He could have told the medical staff at the Busovaca medical centre who, it appears, on some occasions tried to help some of the prisoners by prescribing home treatment. He could have walked away. He had so many opportunities at his disposal, yet he did nothing. Why might that be? In our submission, it is clear. He was a full-fledged supporter of the Bosnian Croatian national cause. He had signed on to a project to ethnically cleanse the Lasva Valley, and he was performing his part of the project. Aleksovski had direct knowledge of what was going on. He was there present when Muslim detainees were taken trench digging. He was there when they were so exhausted from trench digging they collapsed from exhaustion. He was there when they were taken as human shields. He was there when they were beaten. He was there when they were so badly beaten that they needed medical attention. He was there when they had to sleep on wooden pallets. He was there when they were overcrowded into the cells. He was there when it was cold and they did not have sufficient blankets to keep them warm. He was there when they were ill and did not receive adequate medical attention. He had direct knowledge of all of these matters. We are not here trying to argue constructive knowledge. We don't have to. We have ample evidence of his direct knowledge and his personal involvement. In the Celebici judgement, the Trial Chamber said that there had to be some specific information available to a superior which would provide notice of offences committed by his subordinates. In that case, the Trial Chamber noted, however, that the information need not be sufficient to compel the conclusion of the existence of the crimes but sufficient to put him on enquiry of the possible existence of the crimes having been committed. All there needs to exist is information of a sufficiently widespread and notorious nature which, as the section says, "should have enabled him to conclude," but these formulations only have application in those cases where there is no direct knowledge of his presence when the crime was actually being committed. On the evidence of this case, there can be no issue that Aleksovski was the warden or commander of the camp. He clearly admits this himself, but irrespective of what he might say, the evidence of his position of authority is overwhelming. As was noted in the Celebici judgement at paragraph 750, the Trial Chamber states: "It seems inescapable from the testimony of all the detainees that they acknowledged Mucic as the prison camp commander. The detainees came to this conclusion because Delic called him commander or because Mucic himself introduced himself as commander or because his behaviour towards the guards was that of commander. Concisely stated, everything about Mucic contained the indicia and hallmark of a de facto exercise of authority. Even in the absence of explicit de jure authority, a superior's exercise of de facto control may subject him to criminal liability for the acts of his subordinates. Where the position of Mucic manifests all the powers and functions of a formal appointment, it is idle to contend otherwise." In paragraph 261, they say that the precise scope of the superior's duties are irrelevant to the issue. There was evidence of his presence in the camp and the exercise of his de facto authority over prison camp personnel. In this case, it would be hard to find a more convincing case of superior responsibility than that of Mr. Aleksovski. On the evidence that you have heard in this case, it is, in our submission, frankly, incontestable. Turning to another matter, Your Honours, relating to lesser included charges. The issue of whether the Tribunal has authority to find an accused person not guilty of a serious charge as specified in the indictment but, on the evidence, guilty of a less serious charge not specified in the indictment is not without controversy. The Tadic Trial Chamber decided that it did not have the authority to find the accused person guilty of a less serious charge in those circumstances where the accused had been acquitted of a far more serious charge. In the Celebici case, the Trial Chamber took the opposite view. In paragraph 866, they say that, when dealing with the charges in that case: "Nonetheless, it is clear that Delic and Landzo were, at the very least, the perpetrators of heinous acts which caused great physical suffering to the victim." They then say: "It is a principle of law that a grave offence includes a lesser offence of the same nature. Accordingly, the Trial Chamber finds Delic and Landzo not guilty of the charges of wilful killing and murder but finds them guilty of wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body and health, a grave breach of the Geneva Conventions." Having regard to the fact that the International Criminal Tribunal is not restricted to any one system of law, it would be entirely appropriate, in my submission, for the Trial Chamber to follow and expand upon the course set by the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case and introduce this principle of lesser included offences in relation to these matters. Turning now, Your Honours, to briefly touch upon matters raised in the Defence submission that you have before you, their written submission, in paragraph 2.1, the Defence assert that the Prosecutor has not proved a state of international armed conflict or partial occupation in the territory of Busovaca municipality in the period from January till the end of May 1993. They are quite right. We have not been that specific. The reason for this is because, in our submission, we do not, as a matter of law, have to prove this for the grave breach provisions of the Geneva Conventions to apply. It has not been stated in the indictment that we would prove this nor that we ever asserted that we would prove this. The Prosecutor did however, in paragraph 22.1 of the indictment, allege that a state of international armed conflict did exist in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant times, and we have certainly proved this. With respect to, as I have said, the parameters of the conflict, we are not here examining the Busovaca/Vitez municipality and the particular forces involved in the conflict in that area to determine whether the conflict was international or internal. Rather, the question is, was the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina international? There are other matters that the Defence consider we have not proved referred to in part 2 of the Defence submissions, but either as a matter of law, there is no obligation to prove such matters, or alternatively, the matters have been more amply proved in accordance with the obligations imposed upon the Prosecutor. For the purpose of my submission, it's not necessary for me to dwell on these matters, as they are primarily factual and will be discussed in greater detail by my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda. The Defence, in their submission, pages 14 and 15, agree with the Prosecution that the accused started to work as a warden of the Kaonik detention camp in January 1993 and exercised control over the camp, but they argue that because we did not prove that he was a member of the HVO, that he had no rank or that he was a military commander, that because of this, somehow this is fatal to our case. The Prosecution never alleged that he had a military rank or that he was a military commander. This was not alleged in the indictment. It was not alleged in the indictment because it does not, as a matter of law, have to be proved as a legal requirement by the Prosecution. Again, in the Celebici judgement, page 261, the Trial Chamber refer to the Defence argument in that case that the commander of Celebici, Mucic, had no formal command like the position here; therefore, Mucic could not be held responsible. They refer to the Defence concession that Mucic did what he could within the limit of his authority. The Trial Chamber, nevertheless, concluded that he was in a position to help detainees, and they say: "There is no suggestion ... that superior authority can only be vested formally in written form ... individuals in positions of authority, whether civilian or military structures, may incur criminal responsibility on the basis of their de facto as well as de jure position as superiors. The mere absence of formal legal authority to control the actions of subordinates should therefore not be deemed to defeat the imposition of criminal responsibility." On page 17 of the Defence submissions, it is argued -- I have to go even slower, Your Honours. It is argued that the Prosecution failed to prove that the accused had knowledge of the commission of offences contrary to the Geneva Conventions or that persons were about to commit such crimes. This is, in our submission, an extraordinary submission considering the evidence. Aleksovski himself admitted that offences contrary to the Geneva Conventions were being committed. He was present when such offences were committed. He would have to have been in a coma not to know what was going on in the Kaonik camp during the relevant period. The Defence go on, at the bottom of page 17, to make an entirely unsubstantiated comment that: "... Analysing the witnesses' testimonies of the disputable facts, the unquestionable impression is that the witnesses have been instructed and manipulated by the secret police AID controlled by the Bosnian Muslims which is indicated by the fact that their depositions were taken in the premises of the police in a pre-trial proceeding."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, could you please slow down a little bit -- that is why I'm interrupting you -- because we can give you some extra time if necessary at the end as a present.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm more concerned about my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, cutting into his time, Your Honours, but I will certainly slow down. I was just referring to the fact that the Defence, in their submissions, had said that the impression was that the witnesses had been manipulated by the secret police. They base this on the fact of where the pre-trial statements were taken. Well, Your Honours, the pre-trial statements were taken by professional investigators of the Office of the Prosecutor. The witnesses were, in no way, manipulated. There is absolutely no evidence of this. In our submission, this is a cowardly allegation, having regard to the fact that the witnesses were never cross-examined on this matter. They came to The Hague, exposed themselves for cross-examination, but the Defence did not confront them with this unfounded allegation. They waited until the witnesses returned, and behind their backs, they make these comments. On page 18 of the Defence submission, the Defence complain that we have not produced any medical evidence of death. In our submission, there is one very good reason for this, and that is because Mr. Aleksovski has not been charged with killing anyone. With respect to the evidence of serious injury to body or health, again there has been extensive evidence of this, but there's no requirement at all of this having to be supported by medical testimony when one has direct eyewitness testimony. Both in Tadic and Celebici, the Trial Chambers have held that corroboration of evidence is not a customary rule of international law and, as such, should not ordinarily be required by the International Tribunal. That is paragraph 594 of Celebici and 539 of Tadic. Accordingly, the eyewitness testimony is sufficient on its own to establish such matters, and medical or expert testimony of such matters is not required. Interestingly enough, the Defence do not dispute the fact that the police from the HVO were taking Muslim prisoners from the Kaonik prison camp to the front line to dig trenches. As I mentioned before, they go on to say that they consider it established that Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic were killed (7 February 1993) when they were forcibly taken to Kula to dig trenches for the HVO. All they can say with regard to this is that the accused, the military police, and the competent court took appropriate action. The accused had knowledge, he had the capacity to take action if he so desired, and he knew just how dangerous it was for Muslims to be taken from the prison and made to dig these trenches. This, in our submission, is a very clear and further admission of guilt on the part of the accused. When dealing with the classifications of the conflict as "international" and the status of "protected persons" in the "Legal Aspects and Categories" part 4 of the Defence submission, the Defence rely almost exclusively on the Tadic judgement, which, as Your Honours know, was not followed in the Celebici decision. Interestingly enough though, on page 41 of the Defence submission, they do concede that the Defence has no doubt that the alleged victims covered by the indictment are civilians. Just for a moment, I might turn to the indictment itself. From a reading of the Defence submission, one gains the impression that the Defence are under the misapprehension that the Prosecutor has set out to prove all allegations in the indictment which are directed to persons who were originally co-accused with Mr. Aleksovski. Of course, this indictment is a multi-accused indictment, and the accused has been severed from the indictment and a separate trial has been held. A good many of the allegations in the indictment apply exclusively to the other accused and have no application to the accused Mr. Aleksovski. However, there are some paragraphs that do apply. For example, paragraph 1: In our submission, the Prosecution has proved the allegation concerning the conflict as particularised in this paragraph. Some of the allegations in the paragraph are more particulars and do not need to be proved beyond a reasonable doubt but nonetheless have been proved. Paragraph 7: Particulars as to the accused have been proved to the level of the required standard. Paragraph 20: The Prosecution has proved beyond a reasonable doubt that the accused was the commander of Kaonik at the relevant time; he was in a superior position to others in the camp; he exercised the role of commander by meeting with officials of the International Community. The Prosecution has also proved to the required standard that he had an understanding of the Geneva Conventions. Paragraph 21 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I apologise, but we have to wait a little longer for the French interpretation which is lagging behind considerably. Therefore, French booth, will you continue up to the point where Mr. Niemann stopped? Mr. Niemann, you may continue now, and try to go a little more slowly to avoid the same situation from recurring. I apologise, Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Paragraph 21: The Prosecution has proved that Aleksovski exercised control over the Kaonik prison. Paragraph 22.1: The Prosecution has proved to the requisite level that an international armed conflict and partial occupation existed in Bosnia-Herzegovina at the relevant time. Paragraph 22.2: That the alleged grave breaches occurred during an international armed conflict has been proved beyond the required level, in our submission. Paragraph 22.3: The Prosecution has proved that the crimes charged as crimes against humanity took place as part of a widespread and systematic attack. Paragraph 22.4: That the victims were protected persons under the Geneva Convention has also been proved. Paragraph 22.5: That the accused is bound by those conventions. Paragraph 31: It has been established that, at the relevant times, the accused Aleksovski accepted and detained hundreds of Bosnian Muslim civilians from the HVO and their agents. The civilians, for the most part, came from the municipalities of Vitez and Busovaca. That many of the detainees were subjected to inhumane treatment, which included interrogation, physical and psychological harm, forced labour, including trench digging, and use as human shields, and that some of the detainees were murdered or otherwise killed. Paragraph 37: That the accused was responsible under Article 7(1) and (3) of the Statute of the Tribunal for: Inhumane treatment, contrary to Article 2(b) of the Statute; wilfully causing great suffering or serious injury to body or health, contrary to Article 2(c); and outrages upon personal dignity, contrary to Article 3 of the Statute. All these matters have been proved to the requisite level of proof such that, in our submission, the accused is guilty as charged. Turning to the question of sentencing, if Your Honours please. Again, looking at the decision in Celebici, in paragraphs 1237 to 1248 of their judgement, the Trial Chamber provides an interesting discussion of its sentencing criteria with respect to Mucic, who was the commander of the Celebici prison camp and most analogous to Mr. Aleksovski. Unlike the situation with Mr. Aleksovski, the Chamber acknowledges that there was no credible evidence at trial that Mucic actually participated in acts of violence against prisoners and that he may have occasionally prevented such acts of violence. But the Celebici Trial Chamber does not use this distinction to reduce Mucic's culpability per se. On the contrary, in paragraphs 1242 and 1243 of the judgement, they observe that: "... conditions of detention in the Celebici prison camp were harsh and indeed inhumane ... No one appeared to care whether the detainees survived. These were the conditions perpetrated by Mucic, who was the commander of the Celebici prison camp after its creation ... Mr. Mucic was responsible for the conditions in the prison camp and the unlawful confinement of the civilians there detained. He made no effort to prevent or punish those who mistreated the prisoners or even to investigate specific incidents of mistreatment including the death of detainees ..." Thus, for the purposes of liability under Article 7(3), Mucic's individual criminal responsibility was unrelated to whether he directly participated in acts of violence against prisoners or not. This is consistent with the International Committee of the Red Cross commentaries that describe how superiors are often in unique positions to reduce suffering during wartime. In paragraph 1248 of the Celebici judgement, they observed: "On the whole, the Trial Chamber has taken into consideration the conduct of the accused within the situation when he was in possession of considerable authority and was exercising the power of life and death over the detainees in the prison camp. "The Trial Chamber has taken into account the fact that the accused has not been named by any of the witnesses as an active participant in any of the murders or tortures for which he was charged with responsibility as a superior ... The scenario thus described would suggest the recognition of individual failing as an aspect of human frailty, rather than one of individual malice. The criminal liability of Mr. Mucic has arisen entirely from his failure to exercise his superior authority for the beneficial purpose of the detainees in the Celebici prison camp." Mr. Aleksovski, on the other hand, directly participated when beatings were occurring and when interrogations of prisoners took place. He sent prisoners out to the front lines to dig trenches on a daily basis, hid abused prisoners from the International Committee of the Red Cross delegations, and promised one of the guards that Hamdo Dautovic would not leave Kaonik alive. Applying the logic of the Celebici judgement, the repeated malice exhibited by Mr. Aleksovski serves as an aggravating factor that should increase his sentence, even for acts of violence committed by subordinates in which he had no direct participation at all. Aleksovski had the capacity to prevent harm to the prisoners but even more fundamental was his duty to prevent. The accused accepted a mandate from the HVO government and army to run a prison. He enjoyed broad authority over the institution, the prison guards, and the lives of the prisoners. The accused has a university education, and from his prior professional experience, the accused was fully aware of the proper standards for running a prison. He made no serious effort to fulfil his duty and alleviate the suffering and deplorable conditions of the prisoners, although given his dominance over the prison structure and the guards, it would have been relatively easy for him to have done so. Abrogation of the accused's Article 7(3) responsibility as a superior is, in our submission, more culpable than the commission of the specific crimes themselves. That is because, by codifying this theory of superior responsibility in the Additional Protocols to the 1949 Geneva Conventions, the international community established that a superior's fulfilment of this duty was essential to reduce the suffering of war. The culpability of a person who commits a specific offence loses significance, in our submission, in comparison with an accused who controls an entire organisation. Pursuant to Rule 101(B)(ii), the Prosecution asserts that there are no mitigating circumstances or instances of substantial cooperation with the Prosecutor which would earn him any reduction in the sentence that would otherwise be imposed. Having regard to the degree of his direct participation in the commission of these crimes and hence his state of mind, in our submission, his offending was very serious. It has been the practice of the Prosecutor to express her views on what she considers the appropriate sentence should be upon the conviction of the accused. I am accordingly instructed to advise the Chamber that the Prosecutor considers that having regard to all the circumstances of this case, the appropriate sentence, in her view, in the case of Mr. Aleksovski, is that he should serve a sentence of not less than 10 years' imprisonment. If Your Honours please, those are my submissions. I now turn to my colleague, Mr. Meddegoda, who will address you on matters of fact, if Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Niemann. I think that we all are familiar with the capacity of analysis and synthesis by Mr. Meddegoda, and therefore, we are going to give him a 20-minute break for us and before he begins. Therefore, a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: (The accused entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Perhaps a small explanation is required in connection with the delay in the interpretation. Perhaps -- the interpreters need to have the official text of the Celebici judgement to be able to interpret; they need to have an official text. But I think we have overcome that. We have already referred to Mr. Meddegoda's capacity of synthesis, but the present is for the Prosecution as a whole, not only for Mr. Niemann. I want to tell you that we have slightly reorganised the framework of our proceedings so that the Chamber is going to have the morning and the afternoon because we will perhaps need some time for the rebuttal and the rejoinder. Mr. Meddegoda, we are not going to be able to tell in advance your capacity for synthesis, but we do believe in it, so please go slowly because the interpreters need to provide an official interpretation. When you quote a text, then the interpreters need to find the original version of the Celebici judgement or whatever it is you are quoting. Therefore, I think this is very important for the proceedings that we envisage sufficient time in order to be able to do things properly. Therefore, Mr. Meddegoda, take your time knowing that at 6.00, we are going to adjourn for today, but you will be able to continue tomorrow knowing again that counsel for the Defence is also going to have sufficient time. Therefore, tomorrow we will resume at 9.30, and we will work until 1.00 for the morning; and in the afternoon, we are going to resume work at 2.30 and continue until 6.00 p.m., if necessary. Therefore, please go slowly, and this applies to both the Prosecution and the Defence. It is up to you now, Mr. Meddegoda. We are going to listen to you with interest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will fully comply with Your Honours' directive, and if Your Honours please, for my part, I will deal with the factual issues, examining the evidence that has been led before this Trial Chamber. In the course of its case, the Prosecution called 37 witnesses to testify before this Court. It is my submission that the evidence led before this Court establishes beyond reasonable doubt that the accused Zlatko Aleksovski is guilty of the charges alleged against him in the indictment. Your Honours, I now propose to examine the evidence in order to demonstrate that the Prosecution has established the case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt. Vahid Hajdarevic, a Bosnian Muslim resident of Busovaca, testified that he had been mobilised into the Territorial Defence in April of 1992 and had been deployed on the front line in June 1992 and then in September and again in December of that year in order to "defend the integrity of Bosnia-Herzegovina, whereas," if I may quote, "the HVO members at that time were always within certain armed forces ... focused more on obstructing the work of the government in Busovaca and were trying to place the town in a blockade." Thus, from about October of that year, there were various incidents of "mistreatment and harassment, disarming of members of the Territorial Defence, and even plundering and looting of some resources. For instance," the witness said, "I know that some vehicles from us that were going to Slovenia were confiscated by the HVO, so all kinds of looting and plunder occurred. Even before that, there were some minor incidents" which were resolved by negotiation. "But as from October, as far as I can recall ... the political leadership of the HDZ and, of course, with the armed units of the HVO ... took over a number of institutions in the municipality." Recalling the incidents of harassment and mistreatment, it was his testimony that "Muslim intellectuals were taken into custody by the HVO for some sort of interrogation, Muslim coffee shops, shops and property were blown up ..." and on 21st January, 1993, "Mirsad Delija was murdered, thus heightening the tension and causing fear among the Muslim population living in Busovaca." On 24 January, 1993, the witness and his father Sead had been arrested by the HVO at the railway station in Busovaca and taken to the bus station where they were detained together with others, including Remzija Kutic and Mirsad Dizdarevic. Late in the evening, the witness and about nine others had been transferred to Kaonik camp where they had been incarcerated in a small cell. Describing the building as a hangar, he said that the cells were located on either side of a long corridor. He had been detained in three different cells. He described the conditions within the cell as unhygienic. In order to use the toilet, he said, he "had to knock on the cell door, and if the guard who was there saw fit, he would then allow us to go to the toilet." There were no heating facilities in the cell either, nor were there proper facilities to enable the detainees to observe their religious rites and rituals. He said that during the period of his detention, the accused was the camp commander, a fact he learnt having spoken to some of the guards and seeing the accused issue "certain orders to the guards, it was not difficult to conclude this," the witness said. He was one among many detainees who were taken out on labour deployment to dig trenches on the front lines of the HVO in Prosje, Podjele, and Kula. Describing the manner in which detainees would be taken out of their cells for trench-digging and other labour deployment, the witness testified that depending on the needs of the HVO, the guard would start "calling out their names from a list, and you simply had to answer and then the guard would open the door and turn you over to the person who came," who "would then take you to those places and ... you had to do whatever you were told to do." He said that he had to dig trenches for long hours, at times for even 36 hours. " ... as soon as we had been brought to that location ... soldiers systematically mistreated and beat people to find out whether they had any valuables concealed." "During the digging, we were not allowed to stand upright. We had to keep working because if you did stretch your back, then the soldier would hit you either with his rifle butt or would kick you ..." Recalling the pain, humiliation, and suffering when he was beaten by an HVO soldier, resulting in two broken ribs on the right side, Mr. Hajdarevic said, "I had to kneel before him for him to ask me questions ... If he was dissatisfied with the answer, he would kick me like a football." The witness, Your Honour, also referred to the killings of Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic in Kula and the killing of a person nicknamed "Cakara" in Prosje in the course of trench-digging. On the 24th of January, 1993, Witness A was arrested by HVO soldiers and taken to Kaonik camp where he was detained. He described the cell as a very small one with no electric lights. It had a wooden platform about half a metre in height which was the place where people had to sleep. About two or three days into his detention in Kaonik, it was the witness's testimony that the accused, introducing himself as the camp commander, said that "we would be under his jurisdiction." The witness was one amongst many who were taken to the front lines of the HVO to dig trenches and dugouts. He had been taken on four separate occasions, and on all such occasions, there had been sporadic gunfire. On one occasion, he had been subjected to psychological mistreatment by HVO soldiers. He was taken again the next day to a village in the direction of Donja Rovna. The following day again it was the same routine in the area of Donja Solakovici or Milavice where the group had to dig dugouts, trenches, and so on and so on until very late, almost until midnight. The fourth occasion, Your Honours, was in the location of Kula where " ... they told us to take out everything we had in our pockets, money, jewellery from our necks, and to put everything on a pile, and ... they took some things from the pile ..." After that, the group had continued in the direction of Kula, where they kept on digging trenches until about six in the evening, after which they had been taken to an old house where they were subjected to severe mistreatment, torture, and verbal abuse. Recalling this incident, the witness said, "... One of the detainees was first taken and he was beaten outside the house. Then another was taken out. He was also beaten. We could hear him scream. Next it was my turn. I was the third one to be taken out. So they took me outside and ... another soldier hit me in the back with a blunt object and I fell down. He told me to get up, and I tried to get up but I could not at that moment, so he hit me. He kicked me with his military boots again in my nose, and there was blood coming from my nose. He screamed again. He told me to get up, but I could not ... and he again kicked me in the ear, which started to bleed. He kept yelling, telling me to get up, and I couldn't manage to get up, and then he told me to get back into the house ... and as I was getting into the house, he was beating me all the time ... After that, more detainees were taken out, and that was how we were." That is how, Your Honours, he described the first round of beating, if I may call it that. It was a savage and barbaric attack on innocent victims, on innocent civilians who were detained for no reason other than being Muslims. "While I was in that group, since I was bleeding, my friends smeared themselves with my blood so as to make it look as though they had already been beaten," the witness said. "The solders then came into the house and they started beating all of us. One of them had a knife, and he was stabbing detainees with his knife. The other one was using his rifle butt to hit us with. There was one with a very thick metal chain, another one with a club. It lasted about two hours. After that, things went quiet. They forced us to pray, to say the Lord's prayer, to kiss their cross ... After that, Jasmin Sehovic was taken and was beaten up again and we could hear him moan and cry, and after that, we heard some shots from an automatic rifle and it went quiet for several minutes. Then Nermin Elezovic was taken out. He had also received some stabs in the stomach. He was also beaten outside and we could hear him moan and then we could hear shots from an automatic rifle." In addition to Jasmin Sehovic and Nermin Elezovic, a young man from Rogatica had also been stabbed. Witness B, Your Honours, a Bosnian Muslim, said that on the 25th of January, 1993, he and his neighbours had surrendered to the HVO after which the soldiers had mistreated and abused them saying, "Look here. This is all a Croatian area. Only one population, only one ethnic community should be living in this area." Having been brought to the camp, they had been marched into the hangar building "with their hands behind their backs," in which, by this time, there had been about 200 to 300 Muslims already detained, which increased to about 500 the next day. He went on to describe the process of registration and said that "HVO members kept bringing in more Muslims to the hangar, and there were only wooden pallets in that hangar and maybe a blanket that was supposed to be shared by two persons." "While we were in the camp, we got two pieces of bread, one plate for two prisoners. We had to eat from the same plate. It was watery beans. The food either was not salty or very salty. As for water, we would knock on the door of the cell if we were thirsty. If the guard was good, he would ask him for water. At times, the guards would say, "What do you want water for?'" Upon being questioned about the interior of the cell, the witness described in detail its location, its interior, and the facilities or the lack of them. He said that "the cell was located on the right-hand corner next to the lavatory ... on the far side of the hangar" from where he would hear "roll calls and when members of the HVO would call out the name of a Muslim ... the Muslim said which cell he was in, then you would hear beating and you would hear water being splashed across to bring him to life after the beating." Describing his personal experiences, the witness said that on one occasion he and ten other Muslims were taken to Prosje to dig trenches throughout the day until about midnight. The next day, Witness B and 20 others had been taken to Kula where they dug trenches the whole day and the whole night. Upon hearing that the ICRC was visiting the camp, the group of detainees had been brought back to the camp. As soon as the members of the International Committee of the Red Cross had left, there had been another roll call and they had been taken back to Kula to continue digging trenches. Again, they had dug continuously until the next morning. The witness testified that one of the HVO members ordered him to open his mouth and cocked an automatic gun into his mouth. He said, "I somehow managed to move my head away and the gun went off around my shoulder, but none of the bullets hit me. I do not know how the rifle fell from my mouth to my shoulder and went off ..." Not only the witness, other detainees too who were engaged in trench digging had been beaten seriously, gravely beaten up. It was his evidence that, at the time he was detained there, Zlatko Aleksovski introduced himself as the warden of Kaonik camp. Witness D had also been arrested by the HVO with the outbreak of hostilities in Busovaca around the 25th or 26th of January, 1993. Upon arrival in Kaonik, he and the others had been detained in a cell and interrogated by Marko Krilic and a guard named Marko Petrovic. He had seen persons between the ages of 13 and 14 to 65 years detained in the camp. "There was one boy ... from Prosje ... who was there with us and he was between 13 and 14 years of age." Describing the conditions in the camp, the witness said that "the food was just some simply boiled food and two people had to share one plate ... could not take a bath ... could not shave ... 20 or 25 of us used to sleep together in the cell ... Some people would lie down and some people had to sit down and sleep ..." Your Honours, this witness was one of many detainees who were taken for trench digging on numerous occasions. Together with other detainees in his group, he had to dig trenches and dugouts till late at night without food or water, close to the front lines amidst sporadic shooting, "in January, early February," in freezing conditions. "It was very cold, the earth was frozen ... we did not have warm clothes," the witness said. It was in these terrible conditions that this witness and other detainees, including the 13-year-old boy, were forced to dig trenches in Milavice, Prosje, Kovacevac, and Kula, amongst other locations. If I may recount Witness F's evidence, Your Honours, he described the events in Busovaca in the latter half of January 1993 and said that "these were among the worst nights because ugly things were happening, explosions, devices were planted on almost all shops, stores held by Muslims ... There were about 50 shops in the centre of town, so that on the 19th, two or three explosions destroyed two cafes, and on 20th January ... in the evening, again things became nasty, and this could be felt first by the cutting of telephone lines, and we knew straightaway something was about to happen ..." Restrictive measures had also been introduced by the HVO headed by Dario Kordic, Anto Sliskovic, and others directed against the Muslims. He said: " ... not a single Muslim could move around freely ... the only people to move around were HVO policemen and HVO fighters, combatants, so they were the ones who could have done it, no one else," the witness said. Late in the evening of the 20th, the witness's house had been attacked and possessions looted. Again on the 24th of January, there had been shooting, explosions, and shelling with snipers all over the town, and "people panicked, a couple were wounded, a couple were killed, and virtually the entire population was swept by panic ... the HVO soldiers were approaching from all sides ... closer and closer ... it was something quite horrifying," the witness testified. "About 3.30 on that day, 60 to 70 Muslim men had been rounded up" and brought to Kaonik. It was his evidence, Your Honours, that soldiers wearing both the HVO insignia and the HV insignia were in Busovaca during this time. He said that some "were wearing the HVO insignia and I knew them personally. There were soldiers who wore the HV insignia and Runolist Brigade. They had separate accents. They were not locals from Busovaca." Your Honours will see that this witness is very clear in his evidence that there were soldiers from the Croatian army whom he called foreigners who were not from the area, who were operating alongside the HVO soldiers during this time. In answer to specific questions, the witness reiterated that he saw soldiers wearing both the HV and the HVO insignia on 26 January, 1993. Upon being brought to the hangar, they had been lined up against a wall and searched, and at that moment, the accused, Mr. Aleksovski, addressing them had said: "Do not fear. You will not miss a hair from your head." The first night spent inside the hangar on the concrete floor had been horribly cold. At one point, a few soldiers came in and took out several young men. Referring to the guards in the camp, the witness said that they were all soldiers. "The guard was a soldier too. He also had insignia belonging to the HVO on him. They were wearing parts of a camouflage uniform, either the trousers or the jackets." He had experienced different things from the very moment he got there. Let us say, the witness said: "Right after dark, maybe half an hour later, I would be brought out into the hallway and I would be beaten up. This would happen every night. I was brought out mostly by one person into the hallway. He must have received some instructions. He had my description because he knew exactly who I was. So he would simply bring me out of the cell. The cell door would not even close, and I would already be beaten, and I would get bloody. He kept coming back every night and beating me. Fortunately, he beat, for the most part, with his hands and he kicked me. He did not use any other instruments. He would kick and beat me with his hands ... and beat me up badly." Your Honours, the witness also described what happened to him when he and another detainee were taken to the building of the Intervention Squad at the entrance to the camp. Narrating his experience, the witness said: "The third day after I was detained in the cell, I was selected and another guy. We were taken to the building at the entrance ... for some form of informative interview, at least that is what we were told. A young soldier ... took us to the entrance of the camp. We were immediately shut up in a cell ... the other man was taken away. I was left behind sitting on a military bed. "Ten or fifteen minutes later, this young man was brought back after being beaten up. Then I was taken. I was taken upstairs and there was a room, a somewhat larger room, and in the middle of the room there was a table ... At the table, two men were sitting, two fighters, soldiers whom I knew personally very well. In fact, I was glad to see them," he said. "However, I was shortly to be disappointed. They offered me cigarettes and coffee and I accepted. Then some sort of conversation started, but let me add that at this table, there were six or seven various types of sticks, wooden, rubber, steel, even police truncheons. I was on the chair at one end of the table, and after the cigarette and the coffee, the questioning started. "They asked me questions about all kinds of things, even about certain Croats who socialised with us. After each answer, the three men who were standing behind my back would hit me with whatever they could get hold of. Perhaps the easiest ... were their kicks with their boots. This lasted three and a half hours. There were some terrible moments. "At one point in time, Marelja walked in, the man who had beat me every night. He hit me with his fist in the face, so he fractured my jaw. After about three hours of this torture, one of these men pushed my head back and put a knife against my throat. I tried to push my neck against that knife. I did not care any more," the witness said. The witness also, Your Honours, described his experiences with trench digging in places of Gavrine Kuce near Putis, where he had spent the whole night digging and the next day until about noon. In the course of trench digging, the witness said: "Around twelve, three of the soldiers who kept coming every five to ten minutes would hit me with their boots, with their hands ... Then around twelve, these three finally came together and they sat near me." "The three of them," he said, "were soldiers wearing HVO insignia. One of them took a piece of newspaper and he rolled it up into some kind of torch and set it aflame, and the other one came behind me and started burning off my beard, which was about two or three centimetres long at the time. After this burning, maybe an hour passed and I continued to dig. They did not give me any water. I asked for some, but it would have been better if I had not because I got more blows over my back for that. "Two of them then came back and took off my hat from me. They put it on a stick, and when they managed to singe it about 70 per cent ... they ordered me to eat it. I was already fatigued because of all of the work. I had not any water, but I had to eat this hat. If I stopped or stalled or tried to get out of it, I would get a blow, a kick, or I would be hit ..." Referring to his release in an exchange organised by the International Committee of the Red Cross, the witness said that the exchange was delayed because of these two men who had been killed in the night between the 7th and the 8th. The Red Cross insisted on finding them, but they were not to be found. At the exchange, there were quite a number of them. All the guards were present. Sliskovic was present. Aleksovski was present. "All of them were present," the witness said. Your Honours, while corroborating other Prosecution witnesses, Witness C testified about his arrest by HVO forces on 27 January, 1993. He also testified about the subsequent detention and maltreatment in Kaonik camp. Your Honours, I do not intend to go into the details of the witness's testimony, except to say that his testimony on these points are consistent with the testimony of other Prosecution witnesses. In the cell where he and his son were detained, there had been about 18 to 20 detainees and the conditions had been very bad. During the detention, because he had been badly beaten and could not sleep at all and did not have room enough to lie down, he would simply sit in the cell and listen to the cries and moans coming from the corridors. As the witness had been suffering from great pain resulting from the beatings, at his request, he had been taken to the Busovaca health centre. In response to a question as to whether he was given any treatment at the health centre, the witness responded: "I cannot really say that it was any help at all." Testifying further, Your Honours, the witness said that the guards and camp officials permitted people from outside to enter the cells and beat the prisoners, and he identified the accused Zlatko Aleksovski as the commander of the camp. Testifying about the breakout of the conflict between the HVO and the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina around 27 January, 1993, Witness L said that, after his arrest, he had been beaten and mistreated by HVO soldiers. He had been taken to Bare from where he had been brought to the bus station in Busovaca and then taken to Kaonik camp. This was his first stint of detention in Kaonik where he was detained until 8 February, 1993. The day after he was brought to Kaonik camp, a group of about 20 detainees, including the witness, had been taken to Podjele to dig trenches. They dug throughout the day until about 8.00 in the night without any rest and then again from 10.00 till the next morning. Witness L's second stint of detention, Your Honours, commenced when he and Witness M were arrested by HVO soldiers who attacked his village on 16 April, 1993. Upon arrival in Kaonik, Zlatko Aleksovski, the accused, introduced himself as the camp commander. He was waiting with several more guards. They had been put into a cell whereupon members of the HVO military police, Zarko and Miro, had started mistreating them. "We were lying on the pallets. They jumped on the pallets and started hitting us and kicking us in the back, in the kidney area, and in the head." Having mistreated the two detainees for some time, they had left saying they would be back. As promised, Zarko and Miro had come back, and Miro had started beating his colleague whilst Zarko stood by watching. At this stage, Your Honours, it was the witness's evidence that the accused Aleksovski had admonished Zarko by saying "What are you waiting for? Why do you not act in the same way as Miro," and then Zarko had started hitting him. These two men had mistreated them again and some time later for the third time. Then came Goran Medjugorac, an HVO member who "started mistreating me ... beatings, blows mainly in the kidney area and the head." He also had been subjected to mistreatment and torture by Anto Cakic "who ordered me to stand at attention ... He would come in every 15 minutes to check whether I was still standing, and when he came, he would occasionally hit me with his leg or with his fist ..." The witness, Your Honours, also testified about the procedure of selecting detainees for trench digging and his own trench digging experiences in Carica, Strane, Kula, Loncari, and Polom. In Strane, there had been sniper fire, and bullets had whizzed past them. At all these locations, they had to dig trenches from morning till late in the evening. He described the conditions of detention as being "very bad." The food was described as "horrible," and he had not had a shower throughout this period. He also said that "anybody could come at any time to abuse" the detainees. His colleague, Your Honours, Witness M, who had also been apprehended at the same time, corroborated the testimony of Witness L. He referred to incidents of beating and referred, in particular, to an incident when two soldiers savagely beat him at the instance of the accused Aleksovski "who had been there all the time," the witness said. That day, he had been beaten six times, and on one occasion, he had lost his consciousness. His "whole body had been black and blue down to the ankles, and up to my neck, there were visible bruises all over my body." This beating, he said, was described as "a dance party." Your Honours, whilst the testimonies of Witnesses L and M are consistent, I submit that they also corroborate each other on material particulars. He was also amongst detainees who were taken to Strane, Loncari, Putis, Kula, Solakovici, Carica, and Polom to dig trenches in hazardous conditions and subjected to abuse, merciless beatings, and severe mistreatment while being engaged in trench digging. At Strane, he had been whipped and beaten. He said that "... throughout the period I spent at Kaonik camp, I was taken to dig trenches and do other forced labour," as a result of which "once I had on my two palms 56 blisters ... and not once from the moment that I was captured on 16 April until I left on 19 June 1993, not once did I have a bath ... we did not even wash our hands, only when we went to the toilet, if you had a chance and if the guard would let you wash your hands and maybe your face ... What clothing I had on me, that was what I took away with me, the vest I wore throughout that time rotted, it fell apart, it was rotten, so I threw it away while I was still in the camp ... I never had any change of clothing ..." Recalling his release from Kaonik, the witness testified that the accused addressing him and his colleague said: "You will be rewarded if you come back here. You will not get out alive again," but "thank God, this wish of the gentleman did not come true," the witness said before Your Honours. Testifying further before this Chamber, the witness said that though the conditions in the camp were bad, "nobody dared talk about these," even with the ICRC. Even after the detainees including the witness were registered by the International Committee of the Red Cross and the accused was advised by the ICRC that the detainees "must not be taken to do labour where we are not safe, and especially not to the front lines, and to do forced labour such as we had been doing," that same night, about midnight, they had been taken to Strane to dig trenches. Witness M, Your Honours, was aware of Arab prisoners who were beaten more severely than others. One detainee whom he identified as "the Arab from Syria" "was in a horrible condition ... he had been beaten and mistreated ... it was terrible -- from early May up until my exchange ... he was beaten up every day, he was abused, different men took turns in doing these things to him." The witness also said that when ICRC officials visited the cells in the camp, the accused denied them access to cell number 4, saying that "that was some kind of storage room ... that there was no need to look into that room, that there was no one there ... and did not have the key ..." Witness N, Your Honours, also a Bosnian Muslim, suffered the same fate in Kaonik camp. Witness N said that the accused, who was the warden of Kaonik prison, said that the detainees "are now under my authority." This witness, Your Honours, testified about the use of detainees as human shields. He said that the following afternoon, 15 detainees, including the witness, were called out by Marko Krilic, tied into three groups of five each, and then taken to be used as human shields. They had been taken to Skradno, where they had to walk towards the village followed by HVO soldiers. Then they had been taken to Strane where again they had been used as a human shield. On this occasion, HVO soldiers had been firing from behind them towards Strane. He had also been taken to dig trenches, during which they had been subjected to abuse and mistreatment by HVO soldiers, as he said, who "beat us with rifle butts, with shovels, it was indescribable," he said. "There were moments when one felt like crying ... and there were moments when you wanted to die ..." They had been "completely exhausted by this time. There were people with fractured ribs ... There was no person who had not been either abused or badly beaten." Witness O, Your Honours, who also testified under pseudonym, was also used as a human shield in Skradno, Strane, and he described the shooting that went on as they were being used as human shields in Strane. The next day, he had been taken to Merdani again to be used as a human shield. Witnesses P and Q, Your Honours, again Bosnian Muslim civilians who had been arrested by HVO soldiers and detained in Kaonik camp, corroborated the testimony of other witnesses about their use as human shields in Skradno, Strane, and Merdani. Witness P said that his release from Kaonik was "like his second birthday." Witness Q had also been taken to dig trenches and dugouts in hazardous conditions in Kula and Prosje, where he had been beaten and mistreated. Your Honours, Witness R also narrated his experiences during detention in Kaonik camp. Having been arrested by the HVO in January of 1993, he had been detained, during which time he had been taken to Merdani to be used as a human shield. It was then Witness R's testimony, Your Honours, that the camp commander, Aleksovski, was standing by when the detainees were called out to be used as human shields. Witness S, Your Honours, also a Bosnian Muslim civilian, had been arrested by the HVO on 25th January, 1993, and taken to Kaonik where he was detained. He too had been taken to Skradno and Strane to be used as a human shield. He said during the period of his detention, he had been taken to Donja Polje, Donja Solakovici, and Bare to dig trenches for the HVO. On one occasion, he had spoken to the accused requesting that he be spared from trench-digging as there were blisters on his hands. The accused had not responded, "he had simply passed by" and "I was taken out for digging again," the witness said. Your Honours, testifying about the pre-war situation in general and life in Busovaca in particular, Edin Novalic said that it was more than cordial and normal, with very cordial and friendly relations between members of the different ethnicities. Differences had become visible only after the first multi-party elections in 1991. "Differences were becoming more and more profound in everyday life. HVO posters were visible all through the town, and little by little, they started arming themselves illegally. They became stronger and stronger every day, and at a certain moment in the second half of 1992, the HVO, through the use of force, took over complete power in the town of Busovaca with barricades all over the town." In the witness's opinion, it was "Dario Kordic and Anto Sliskovic who were the major players in Busovaca." By January of 1993, conflict had erupted in Busovaca, with Muslim shops and businesses being attacked by means of explosive devices on the night of the 22nd of January. On 23rd January, Muslims, including the witness, had been arrested and taken to Kaonik camp where they had been subjected to the routine of search and detention in the presence of the accused. Corroborating the evidence of the use of Muslim prisoners as human shields, Mr. Novalic testified that he had been taken to Strane and Merdani to negotiate the surrender of the two villages. Another Bosnian Muslim civilian, Meho Sivro, from the village of Stojkovici, had been arrested on 13 April and brought to Kaonik camp. During the period of his detention, the witness had been taken to Jelinak on two occasions to dig trenches. On the first occasion, he said it had been very dangerous when "all of us could have got killed because a burst of fire was opened on" our group of five or six while we were being taken by an HVO soldier. The second time "it was the same village," and they had dug throughout the night till dawn when "the BH army started shelling the village." Some explosions could also be heard. With the ensuing panic, the commander had ordered that the group of detainees be taken away and killed. The witness had "thought it was the end, that we would all be executed." Proceeding towards Loncari, the witness said, "We almost reached the village when the shooting started from HVO weapons ... the bullets were hitting the trees and the shrapnel ... started showering upon us." The witness described quite vividly how he made use of the ensuing chaos and panic to make good his escape, running across fields, jumping over fences, and sliding down slopes until he got to the territory controlled by the BH army. Your Honours will recall the emotional strain on the witness's face when recounting those events and when he said that as a result of this, he had to undergo surgery on his right arm, which has only 60 per cent use for him now. Another Bosnian Muslim witness, Your Honour, Rasim Garanovic, said that at the beginning of 1993, things started to change when "strange things began to happen ... most probably from Zagreb ... through the HVO, the HVO police. They started to ignore their neighbours, the Bosniaks ... with less and less contact with the Bosniaks" with an HVO "checkpoint right next to my house." On 14 April, 1993, he had been arrested, and on his way to Busovaca, he had passed a checkpoint held by the Croatian army with RPGs and other weapons. Upon arrival in Kaonik camp after the routine registration and search, the witness had been detained in the hangar, and, describing the night in the hangar, he said, "The night was very fatal for me. It was very cold and I got cramps, very bad cramps, in my chest." Some people had been seated on pallets but most had sat on concrete and "I remained on concrete." "Then they put some kind of imaginary line and said that whoever crossed this line would be shot ..." The next morning, after he had complained that he was feeling unwell, he had been taken before the camp commander, Zlatko Aleksovski, who had questioned him and then he had been put into a cell where he had been detained throughout his period of detention. He testified, Your Honours, about detainees being taken out for trench-digging on a daily basis, about beatings which were "very frequent or relatively frequent." He said that the names were read out from a list that was brought out from Aleksovski's office. "I did hear beatings rather far away in the other cells. Some people were tortured in the corridor ... we just listened when this was happening, when they were beaten up ... from my cell, two guys were taken out and beaten up." They were Mustafa Hodzic and (redacted). This is "imprinted in my memory because they beat them so fiercely that (redacted) had a serious spinal injury ... still suffering from the consequences ..." (redacted)- told him that "even Zlatko had hit him once or twice as he passed by." Your Honours, another witness -- very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think this is a good time to interrupt our work for today. I should like to remind you that tomorrow we will meet again here not at 9.00 a.m. but at 9.30. We must bear this in mind because that means we have an extra half hour to work or to sleep, depending on everybody's preference. The hearing is adjourned. I apologise, Mr. Mikulicic. You wanted to say something?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. It is my mistake if I indicated too late that I wanted to take the floor. But in accordance with my client's request, Mr. Aleksovski, I would like to ask whether he could be allowed to go out into the fresh air after he returns from the courtroom today, and tomorrow he has a whole day of hearings, and for his medical condition, could he be allowed to have a walk in the fresh air after he returns from the courtroom to the detention unit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I think this can be granted, but I would like to ask the registrar, Mr. Marc Dubuisson, to tell us the procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I don't think there will be the least problem in meeting this request.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Therefore, it is granted in the interests of Mr. Aleksovski's health.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Now we can adjourn until tomorrow.
